ety.text: Via late Middle English can, chan from Old French chan, from Medieval Latin chanis, from Turkic *qan, contraction of *qaɣan. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰴𐰍𐰣 (qaɣan), and Mongolian хаан (xaan), possibly from Rouran. Sense 1 (ruler in the Middle Ages) after Genghis Khan, from Middle Mongol ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ (qaɣan). Doublet of khagan.
From Arabic خَان (ḵān, “inn, caravanserai, hotel”) and Persian خان (xân, “inn, caravanserai”).

senses.d: A ruler over various Turkic and Mongol peoples in the Middle Ages.
A noble or man of rank in various Muslim countries of Central Asia, including Afghanistan.
Synonym of caravanserai (particularly in Middle Eastern contexts)
Synonym of fonduk (“inn or hotel in Middle Eastern contexts”).

ety.text: From Middle French chan, from Old French chan, from Medieval Latin chānus, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.
From Old French chan, from Medieval Latin chanis, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cãa, from Latin cānam, feminine accusative singular of cānus. Compare Spanish cana.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese can, from Latin canis, canem. Compare Galician and Spanish can.
